name: Maghe Sankranti Mela, Jorethang
when: Mid-January, from the 1st of Magh in the Nepali calendar (about 14–15 January)
summary: Jorethang's Maghe Sankranti mela, held on the Rangeet riverbank since 1961, is one of the biggest Nepali community festivals in Sikkim. It opens with ritual bathing on the first of Magh, around 14 January, and runs for several days as a fair with stalls, food, music and rides.
body: Maghe Sankranti marks the first day of Magh in the Nepali Vikram Samvat calendar, when the sun enters Makara, Capricorn, and the cold of Poush begins to give way. The Wikipedia article on the festival describes ritual baths at river confluences and festive foods such as sesame sweets, ghee, yam and sweet potato. In Sikkim, Jorethang on the Rangeet is the best-known place to celebrate, and Wikipedia's article on the town dates its mela to 1961.

The day begins early, with families bathing in the Rangeet and offering prayers. Then the riverbank turns into a fair. Stalls sell farm tools, bamboo baskets, clothes, handicrafts and household goods, and food stalls fry sel roti and sell the season's sweets. Cultural programmes, folk music and amusement rides run through the fair days, drawing visitors from across South and West Sikkim and from the Darjeeling hills across the river.

For visitors, the mela is a chance to see a large, cheerful community festival rather than a staged show. It is crowded and noisy in the best way. Traffic into Jorethang slows to a crawl at peak times, so many people stay in Namchi, 18 km uphill, and come down by taxi. Exact dates and the programme are announced by the organisers each year; check current status before you travel.
tips: Book rooms in Namchi early for mela week; Jorethang's few hotels fill with visiting families.
Go mid-morning for the best atmosphere, and keep phones and wallets secure in the crowds.
Try the seasonal foods: sesame and molasses sweets, boiled yam and sweet potato, and fresh sel roti.

faqs.q: When is the Jorethang Maghe Mela in 2027?
faqs.a: Maghe Sankranti usually falls on 14 or 15 January, and the Jorethang mela begins then and runs for several days. The exact dates and programme for 2027 will be announced by the organisers closer to the time. Check current status before you travel, and ask us for confirmed dates when booking.

faqs.q: How old is the Jorethang Maghe Mela?
faqs.a: Wikipedia's article on Jorethang records that the town's Maghe Sankranti mela dates from 1961, making it one of the longest-running community fairs in Sikkim. It has grown from a riverside gathering for ritual bathing and trade into a multi-day fair with cultural programmes, stalls and rides.

faqs.q: Can tourists join the Maghe Sankranti mela?
faqs.a: Yes. Visitors are welcome to walk the fair, eat at the stalls and watch the cultural programmes. If you join the morning river bath, follow local customs and stay in shallow, calm water near others. Dress modestly, ask before photographing people, and be patient in the crowds.

faqs.q: Where should we stay for the Jorethang mela?
faqs.a: Namchi, 18 km and about 40 minutes uphill, is the best base, with rooms for every budget and cooler nights. Jorethang itself has only a few basic hotels that fill quickly in mela week. A reserved taxi between Namchi and Jorethang costs about ₹1,000–1,500 each way, indicative.

name: Pang Lhabsol at Ralang Monastery
image_query: Pang Lhabsol cham dance Sikkim monastery
when: Aug–Sep, 15th day of the 7th Tibetan month (lunar)
community: Bhutia and Lepcha, with all of Sikkim's Buddhists
summary: Pang Lhabsol honours Kangchenjunga, worshipped in Sikkim as Dzö-nga, the guardian deity of the land, and recalls the blood-brotherhood oath between the Lepcha and Bhutia. Ralang Monastery near Ravangla marks the day with masked cham dances in its courtyard, drawing families from across South Sikkim.
body: Pang Lhabsol falls on the 15th day of the 7th month of the Tibetan calendar, usually in late August or September. It is a festival found only in Sikkim. It honours Kangchenjunga as the protector of the land and is closely tied to the tradition of the oath of brotherhood sworn between the Lepcha chief Thekong Tek and the Bhutia ancestor Khye Bumsa at Kabi Lungchok, with the mountain as witness. The state observes it as a public holiday.

Ralang, a Kagyu monastery 6 km from Ravangla, is one of the places where monks perform cham, masked dances, for Pang Lhabsol. Wikipedia's article on Ralang Monastery lists cham on the 15th day of the 7th month, and the monastery's dancers are known for their costumes and the precision of their movements. Dancers represent protector deities and warriors, moving slowly to drums, cymbals and long horns, and the courtyard fills with families who arrive early to find a place.

Pang Lhabsol falls in the monsoon, so pack rain gear and expect slow roads. Ravangla rooms fill quickly that week, so book early. Gangtok holds its own large celebration at the same time, but Ralang offers a village setting and a closer view. Dates follow the lunar calendar and move each year; check current status before you travel. Carry cash for donations and food stalls.
tips: Arrive early with a cushion, water, a hat and a rain jacket; the courtyard fills fast and weather changes quickly.
Never walk across the dance ground, and ask before photographing monks or elders.
Book Ravangla or Kewzing rooms well ahead; the festival falls in a short week of high local demand.

faqs.a: Pang Lhabsol falls on the 15th day of the 7th Tibetan month, which in most years lands in late August or September. The Sikkim government's holiday list announces the date each year, and monasteries confirm their dance programmes shortly before. Check current status before you travel, and ask us for the confirmed date.

It honours Kangchenjunga, worshipped in Sikkim as Dzö-nga, the guardian deity of the land, and recalls the oath of brotherhood between the Lepcha and Bhutia peoples, sworn at Kabi Lungchok with the mountain as witness. It is unique to Sikkim and a state holiday.

faqs.q: Can visitors watch the cham dances at Ralang?
faqs.a: Yes. The courtyard is open to the public, and visitors are welcome as long as they behave respectfully. Sit where locals indicate, keep off the dance ground, switch off flash and ask before close-up photographs. There is usually no ticket; a small donation is appreciated.

faqs.q: How do we reach Ralang Monastery for Pang Lhabsol?
faqs.a: Ralang is 6 km from Ravangla, about 20 minutes by car. Ravangla is about 3 hours from Gangtok and 1 hour from Namchi. On festival day traffic and parking are slow, so leave early. Pang Lhabsol falls in the monsoon, so allow extra time for road slips.

name: Maha Shivaratri at Char Dham, Solophok
when: Feb–Mar, 14th night of the dark fortnight of Phalguna (lunar)
community: Hindu communities of Sikkim and pilgrims from across India
summary: Maha Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva, is the biggest day of the year at Siddhesvara Dham on Solophok hill above Namchi, home to a 108 ft Shiva statue. Devotees come for night-long worship, prayers at the twelve jyotirlinga replicas and the view of the lit statue.
body: Maha Shivaratri falls on the 14th night of the dark half of the Hindu month of Phalguna, usually in February or early March. The Wikipedia article on the festival describes it as a night of fasting, prayer and vigil in honour of Shiva, observed across India and Nepal. In Sikkim, the largest gathering is at Siddhesvara Dham, the Char Dham complex on Solophok hill, which opened in 2011 with a 108 ft statue of Shiva at its centre.

The complex brings together replicas of the four dhams, Badrinath, Jagannath, Dwarka and Rameswaram, and the twelve jyotirlingas, so pilgrims can make a symbolic yatra in a single visit. On Shivaratri the crowds swell from early morning, with families queuing to offer water, milk and bel leaves, and prayers continuing late into the night. The statue of Kirateshwar, a form of Shiva honoured by the Kirat communities, also draws devotees.

Late February is dry and clear in South Sikkim, with cool evenings around 8–12 °C at Solophok, so pack a warm layer for the night. Expect long queues, traffic control on the hill road and crowded hotels in Namchi. Entry rules and timings may change on festival days; check current status before you travel. Carry water and snacks, as stalls near the gate are crowded.
tips: Visit early in the morning or late at night for shorter queues than the midday peak.
Wear modest clothing and easy-to-remove shoes; carry socks for cold stone floors.
Book Namchi hotels early, and expect parking to be some distance from the gate.

faqs.a: Maha Shivaratri falls on the 14th night of the dark fortnight of Phalguna, usually in February or early March. Check the Hindu calendar or the Sikkim government holiday list for the exact 2027 date, and check current status before you travel. Char Dham's special timings for the day are announced locally.

faqs.q: What happens at Char Dham on Maha Shivaratri?
faqs.a: Devotees queue from early morning to offer water, milk and bel leaves at the shrines, pray at the jyotirlinga replicas and keep vigil into the night. The 108 ft Shiva statue is the focus. Expect crowds, long queues and a devotional atmosphere throughout the day and night.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at Char Dham on Shivaratri?
faqs.a: Siddhesvara Dham has charged a small entry fee, around ₹50 per adult, on normal days. Arrangements on Maha Shivaratri may differ, with special queues or timings. Fees and rules are revised from time to time, so treat this as indicative and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do we reach Char Dham from Namchi?
faqs.a: Char Dham is on Solophok hill, about 5–7 km from Namchi market, roughly 15–20 minutes by car. On Shivaratri traffic is controlled and parking can be far from the gate, so allow extra time or walk the last stretch. A local taxi from Namchi costs a few hundred rupees, indicative.
